title: Homeostasis and feedback loops
blurb: Name the parts of a feedback loop and classify any body response as negative or positive feedback from what it does to the original change.
question: During labor, contractions trigger more oxytocin, and more oxytocin makes contractions stronger until the baby is born. When body temperature rises, sweating brings it back down. Which of these is negative feedback, which is positive, and how can you tell?

teach.body: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment despite changes inside and outside the body. Each controlled variable, such as body temperature or blood glucose, has a set point it hovers around. Plain English: the body constantly checks its own readings and makes small corrections, the way you steer to stay in your lane. The corrections run through feedback loops.

teach.caption: The response changes the variable, which the receptor detects again, so the loop keeps running.

head: Part
Job
Temperature example
rows: Compares with set point, sends orders
teach.caption: The control center is often the brain, especially the hypothalamus. Effectors are always muscles or glands.

teach.body: Negative feedback is the most common type. The response opposes the original change, pushing the variable back toward its set point: too hot leads to cooling, too much glucose leads to removal. 'Negative' means opposite in direction, not harmful. Examples: body temperature (sweating or shivering), blood glucose (insulin and glucagon), blood pressure (baroreceptor reflex) and blood calcium.

teach.caption: In the cold the effector changes: skeletal muscles shiver to produce heat. Either way, the change is reversed.

teach.body: In positive feedback the response pushes the variable further in the SAME direction, so the change grows until an end event stops the loop. It is rare and used to finish a job quickly. Examples: childbirth (oxytocin strengthens contractions, which trigger more oxytocin, until birth), the blood clotting cascade (each step activates more of the next until a clot forms) and milk ejection during breastfeeding.

teach.caption: Each turn of the loop makes the change bigger. Only the end event (delivery) breaks the cycle.
Classify by direction: does the response oppose the change or add to it?

teach.body: Jamal, a nursing applicant, runs on a hot afternoon. His body temperature rises (stimulus). Temperature receptors detect it (receptor) and signal his hypothalamus (control center), which compares the reading with the set point and signals his sweat glands (effector). Sweat evaporates, his temperature falls, and the signal fades. The response opposed the change, so this is negative feedback.

teach.text: Positive does not mean 'good' and negative does not mean 'bad'. They describe DIRECTION: positive amplifies the change, negative reverses it. Temperature, glucose, blood pressure and calcium control are all NEGATIVE feedback.

items: Homeostasis: a relatively stable internal environment kept near set points.
Loop: receptor detects, control center compares with set point, effector responds.
Effectors are muscles or glands; the control center is often the hypothalamus.
Negative feedback (most common) reverses the change: temperature, glucose, BP, calcium.
Positive feedback amplifies until an end event: childbirth, clotting, milk ejection.

summary: You can now define homeostasis and trace a feedback loop from receptor to control center to effector. You can also classify any response as negative feedback (reverses the change) or positive feedback (amplifies it until an end event) and name the classic examples of each.

A.q: In a homeostatic feedback loop, which component compares incoming information with the set point?
A.why: The control center (often the hypothalamus) receives the receptor's signal, compares it with the set point and directs the effector.

whyNot.0: The receptor detects the change but does not compare it with the set point.
whyNot.1: The effector carries out the response the control center orders.
whyNot.2: The stimulus is the change itself, not a part that evaluates it.

A.q: Which is an example of positive feedback?
options: Insulin release after a high-sugar meal
Baroreceptor reflex when blood pressure rises
A.why: Oxytocin makes contractions stronger, which triggers more oxytocin, amplifying the change until birth.

whyNot.0: Shivering produces heat to reverse a temperature drop: negative feedback.
whyNot.1: Insulin lowers raised blood glucose back toward the set point: negative feedback.
whyNot.3: The baroreceptor reflex brings raised blood pressure back down: negative feedback.

A.q: Negative feedback mechanisms respond to a change in a controlled variable by
options: reversing it back toward the set point
amplifying it until an end event occurs
shifting the set point to the new value
speeding it up to reach a new balance
A.why: Negative feedback opposes the change, returning the variable toward its set point.

whyNot.1: Amplifying a change until an end event is positive feedback.
whyNot.2: Negative feedback defends the existing set point rather than moving it.
whyNot.3: Speeding up a change adds to it, which is the opposite of negative feedback.

B.q: During a long run in hot weather, Kayla's body temperature rises and she begins to sweat. In this feedback loop, her sweat glands act as the
B.why: Effectors are the muscles or glands that produce the response; the sweat glands secrete sweat to cool the body.

whyNot.0: Receptors detect the temperature change; sweat glands respond to it.
whyNot.1: The control center for temperature is the hypothalamus in the brain.
whyNot.3: The stimulus is the rise in body temperature, not the glands.

B.q: Which body function is regulated mainly by negative feedback?
B.why: After a meal, insulin lowers raised blood glucose back toward its set point, reversing the change.

whyNot.0: The clotting cascade amplifies itself until a clot forms: positive feedback.
whyNot.1: Milk ejection is a positive feedback example.
whyNot.2: Labor contractions are driven by positive feedback through oxytocin.

B.q: Which statement about positive feedback is CORRECT?
options: It is the most common feedback type in the body
It amplifies a change until an end event occurs
It keeps body temperature close to its set point
It is any feedback that benefits the body
B.why: Positive feedback pushes a change further in the same direction until an end event, such as birth, stops it.

whyNot.0: Negative feedback is the most common type; positive feedback is rare.
whyNot.3: Positive refers to the direction of the response, not to whether it is beneficial.

C.q: After a meal, Destiny's blood glucose rises. Her pancreas releases insulin, and her blood glucose falls back toward normal. Which BEST describes this response?
options: Positive feedback, since insulin output increases
Negative feedback, since insulin is a hormone
Positive feedback, since glucose levels change
Negative feedback, since the rise is reversed
C.why: The response (insulin) opposes the original change (rising glucose), returning it toward the set point: negative feedback.

whyNot.0: Insulin output rises, but it drives glucose DOWN, opposing the change; that is negative, not positive, feedback.
whyNot.1: Hormones act in both kinds of loop (oxytocin drives a positive one), so being a hormone does not make it negative feedback.
whyNot.2: Every feedback loop involves a change; what matters is whether the response opposes or amplifies it.

C.q: Which sequence shows the correct flow of information in a homeostatic feedback loop?
C.why: The receptor detects the change, the control center compares it with the set point, and the effector produces the response.

whyNot.0: The effector cannot act before the control center has processed the signal.
whyNot.1: The control center needs input from the receptor before it can act.
whyNot.3: The effector responds last, after the receptor and control center.

C.q: Why is the blood clotting cascade classified as positive feedback?
options: It restores blood volume back to its normal set point
Each step amplifies the next until a clot forms
The hypothalamus detects the cut and orders a clot
It is a response that helps the injured body heal
C.why: Each clotting step activates more of the next, so the change grows until the end event: a formed clot.

whyNot.0: Restoring a variable to its set point describes negative feedback.
whyNot.2: Clotting is not run by the hypothalamus; the classification depends on amplification, not on which organ controls it.
whyNot.3: Being helpful does not define positive feedback; positive means the response amplifies the change.

reteach.title: Think of a home thermostat
reteach.question: A thermostat keeps a house at 70 °F by switching the furnace on and off. Which parts of that system match the receptor, control center and effector?

blocks.body: The thermometer inside the thermostat is the receptor. The thermostat's chosen setting is the set point, and its circuit is the control center that compares the reading with it. The furnace is the effector. When the room cools, the furnace switches on; once the room is warm, it switches off. The response reverses the change: negative feedback. Positive feedback is a microphone squeal, where each loop of sound makes the next louder.

blocks.text: A thermostat never makes a cold room colder. If a response makes the change bigger, like the microphone squeal or labor contractions, it is positive feedback.

explain.body: Receptor detects; control center compares with the set point; effector (a muscle or gland) responds.

test.q: Which structure is MOST likely to act as an effector in a homeostatic loop?
options: A temperature receptor in the skin
A sweat gland in the skin
test.why: Effectors are muscles or glands that carry out the response; a sweat gland is a gland.

whyNot.0: A temperature receptor detects change: it is the receptor.
whyNot.1: The hypothalamus compares readings with the set point: it is the control center.
whyNot.3: The set point is the target value, not a structure that responds.

explain.body: The response opposes the change and returns the variable to its set point. Most loops work this way.

test.q: Shivering when body temperature drops is an example of
options: negative feedback lowering the set point
test.why: Shivering produces heat that opposes the drop in temperature, returning it toward the set point.

whyNot.0: Shivering produces heat rather than raising heat loss, and the loop is negative.
whyNot.2: Amplifying the drop would make the body colder; shivering does the opposite.
whyNot.3: Negative feedback defends the set point; it does not lower it.

explain.body: The response adds to the change until an end event stops it: childbirth (oxytocin), blood clotting, milk ejection.

test.q: Which hormone drives the positive feedback loop of childbirth?
test.why: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary strengthens uterine contractions, which trigger more oxytocin.

whyNot.1: Prolactin drives milk production after birth, not labor contractions.
whyNot.2: Insulin lowers blood glucose in a negative feedback loop.
whyNot.3: Progesterone maintains the endometrium and relaxes the myometrium during pregnancy.

explain.body: Negative: temperature, blood glucose, blood pressure, blood calcium. Positive: childbirth, clotting, milk ejection.

test.q: Which pair are BOTH regulated by negative feedback?
test.why: Blood calcium (PTH and calcitonin) and blood pressure (baroreceptor reflex) are both returned to their set points by negative feedback.

whyNot.1: Blood glucose is negative feedback, but blood clotting is positive feedback.
whyNot.2: Body temperature is negative feedback, but childbirth is positive feedback.
whyNot.3: Blood calcium is negative feedback, but milk ejection is positive feedback.
